fields.expected: I'd want to work on evaluation infrastructure for scientific and AI-generated work. Over the past year I've independently studied how research gets funded and selected, reading the history from patronage to the German research university to Bell Labs to the NIH/NSF project-grant model to newer structures like DARPA, ARPA-H, and Focused Research Organizations, and interviewing researchers, administrators, economists, and science-policy people. I started out thinking grant-writing time was the main constraint on science. Talking to people changed that: I now think the bigger effect is selection, where researchers learn which ideas are legible enough to survive review and stop attempting the ones that aren't. The question that came out of that is what happens when AI makes generation cheap while judgment stays scarce. Reviewers have limited time and domain expertise is expensive, so output can grow much faster than the capacity to assess it. I'd want to build the technical side of that: methodological validation, provenance, uncertainty, reproducibility checks, evidence tracing, and escalation to human experts. Failing that, I'd be happy at an early-stage company building tools that surface things conventional systems miss, which is what pulled me into tSearch and talent discovery.

fields.expected: Estimating sleep without a wearable for ClarityAtlas. The product thesis depended on relating a person's behavior to their sleep, but most of our pilot users at Hopkins didn't own a watch, so the signal we most needed was the one we couldn't measure directly. I built a passive estimation system on top of HealthKit and Core Motion, using phone-interaction patterns plus motion features like step count, gait speed, and movement distribution across the day. The hard part wasn't writing the inference, it was that I had no ground truth. Absence of phone activity can mean sleep, or a dead battery, or a phone left on a desk, and the failure modes look identical in the data. I ended up treating low-confidence windows as unresolved rather than forcing a nightly number, because a confidently wrong sleep estimate would poison every downstream comparison, including the Sleep Twins matching I built on standardized behavioral features and weighted distance. That constraint generalized. I now design systems to say "insufficient evidence" instead of guessing, which is the same principle I later used in tSearch, where missing public work is not scored as negative evidence.

fields.expected: How we got in front of the Johns Hopkins president. During Lighting of the Quads, my cofounders and I realized Ron Daniels was somewhere nearby, so we walked over to Garland Hall and found him through the locked doors. We knocked until someone let us make our case, and we pitched ClarityAtlas on the spot. That turned into a formal meeting months later with him and leadership from the Data Science and AI Institute. I'm proud of it because it's the least technical thing I've done on that project and probably one of the highest-leverage. I had spent most of my time on Swift, Supabase, and the sleep estimation pipeline, and I'd been treating institutional support as something that would follow automatically from a good product. It doesn't. Getting users, getting a pilot approved, and repeatedly explaining why the thing should exist turned out to matter as much as shipping it.

fields.expected: Forward Deployed Software Engineer resonates more. The work I've liked most has involved a specific user and a real constraint I couldn't design around. At Intelehealth I built a resource-availability scoring pipeline in Python across 32 villages, combining facility-tier classification, geospatial distance, Maps and weather data, and I also built an evaluation framework comparing AI-generated clinical outputs against a 4,169-case clinical standard using stratified sampling. That second piece only made sense because clinicians needed to know when not to trust an output. At SAC Nexus I work on the ML core of an anomaly-detection system, and the thing I think about most isn't AUC, it's that an alert system producing too many alerts creates a second problem instead of solving the first, which is why I built learning-to-rank prioritization and a retrieval-augmented explanation layer for analysts. That's the FDE problem shape: the model isn't the deliverable, the decision someone makes with it is. I'd still want to be writing serious infrastructure rather than only configuring, and from what I understand the role allows both.
